speaker: John Ketchum
title: NextEra Energy CEO: Powering AI and Nuclear's Comeback
question: In utility-scale energy development, why do large power developers usually avoid owning and operating AI data centers themselves?
guest: The footprint, the technology specifications, the chips that were being used, and the type of customers they were serving were different for all customers, and we wanted to stick to what we were best at, which is our land development capability. We felt we would be better off buying the land for the power generation facility together with the land for the data center, selling that land to a hyperscaler, and having the generation ready to interconnect to the data center—focusing on building wind, solar, battery storage, fired generation, nuclear, transmission, distribution, and gas pipelines. When you sit down with hyperscalers and ask them what they really want, they want to own and control their own data centers. They want the cybersecurity that goes along with protecting their data for their customers. They know that chips evolve over time and need to be replenished, and they want control over their own destiny in those data centers. So we think we can get far more opportunities out of building the power generation while letting hyperscalers build their data centers, rather than cannibalizing demand by insisting on building both.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Large power developers mostly stay out of data center ownership because it is a fundamentally different business with a different risk profile from the one they and their investors are built for.

Their model rests on building generation assets and selling the output under long-term contracts (PPAs) to creditworthy buyers. That produces stable, predictable cash flows that support cheap project financing. Owning an AI data center would swap that for exposure to tenant leasing risk, uncertain AI demand, and hardware that becomes obsolete in a few years, whereas power plants last for decades.

Data centers also demand capabilities developers lack: chip procurement, cooling and network design, extreme uptime operations, and relationships with hyperscale tenants. The capital intensity is far higher too, since the servers and fit-out cost many times more than the power plant feeding them, which would strain balance sheets and compete with their core pipeline.

Finally, the hyperscalers are their best customers. Competing with them makes little sense when developers can capture value more safely by selling power, land, and grid interconnection, or by partnering with specialist data center operators.

points.why: The response describes specialized capabilities without explaining how technical requirements vary across hyperscalers.
The response omits hyperscalers’ need for direct facility control to protect customer data.
The response frames chip obsolescence as a risk for power developers without linking it to hyperscalers’ need to control hardware replacement.
The response identifies competition with hyperscalers but does not explain that building data centers would cost developers power sales to those customers.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Large power developers usually avoid owning and operating AI data centers because the two businesses have fundamentally different operational demands, risk profiles, and capital structures. Energy developers excel at land assembly, permitting, grid interconnection, and power generation, whereas running an AI facility requires specialized expertise in high-density liquid cooling, fiber networking, cybersecurity, and strict uptime guarantees.

Financially, utility-scale power relies on low-cost project finance backed by predictable, multi-decade power purchase agreements. Conversely, AI data centers require massive capital outlays for rapidly evolving compute and thermal architectures, introducing technological obsolescence and re-leasing risks that clash with traditional energy investors' mandates. Operating facilities directly would also pit power developers against their most creditworthy customers—hyperscalers and colocation specialists—who typically insist on controlling proprietary building designs. Because deliverable electricity is already the primary bottleneck in AI expansion, power developers can capture outsized returns at far lower risk by monetizing "powered land," forming joint ventures, or signing premium long-term power contracts.

The response lists cybersecurity as an operating requirement but does not connect it to hyperscalers’ insistence on direct control to protect customer data.
The response frames evolving compute hardware as an investment risk without linking chip replacement cycles to hyperscalers’ need for direct facility control.

noweb.answer:
Large power developers avoid owning and operating AI data centers primarily due to mismatched risk profiles, capital structures, and core competencies. Power developers rely on low-cost infrastructure financing suited to long-lived generation assets backed by predictable, multi-decade power purchase agreements. Conversely, AI data centers require massive capital outlays on specialized high-density electrical and cooling systems exposed to rapid technological obsolescence and shorter re-leasing cycles, which would shift a developer’s risk profile and raise its cost of capital.

Operationally, permitting power plants, securing grid interconnections, and trading electricity share little overlap with running mission-critical digital facilities that demand strict uptime guarantees, liquid cooling management, fiber connectivity, and tenant servicing. Entering the space would also pit developers directly against hyperscalers and colocation providers—the very creditworthy customers needed to underwrite new generation—while regulated utilities face strict legal barriers against exposing ratepayers to commercial technology risks. Instead, power developers capture stronger risk-adjusted returns by supplying powered land, grid interconnections, and firm electricity while leaving data center ownership to digital infrastructure specialists.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Large power developers usually stay out of owning and running AI data centers because it is a different business with a different risk profile. Their edge is in siting, permitting, interconnection, building generation and signing long-term power contracts. Those assets earn steady, contracted, often regulated returns over 20 to 40 years. A data center depends on fast-depreciating hardware such as GPUs that become obsolete in three to five years. It also brings technology and tenant risk, high capital intensity and specialized operating skills like cooling, uptime management and customer service that power developers don't have.

Owning the facility would also concentrate risk. If one AI tenant's demand fell or financing dried up, both the load and the generation would be stranded together. Utilities face an extra hurdle, because regulators and ratepayers resist utility capital going into speculative, unregulated ventures.

So developers act as power suppliers instead. They sign long-term PPAs, build behind-the-meter or co-located generation, or lease powered land to hyperscalers like Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta. Those companies have the balance sheets and expertise to take on the computing risk, while the developer keeps a bankable, contracted revenue stream.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Large power developers usually avoid owning and operating AI data centers because the two businesses have fundamentally different risk profiles, capital structures, and core competencies. Utility-scale power projects are financed with low-cost, long-term infrastructure capital built around predictable, multi-decade power purchase agreements and 20-to-30-year asset lives. By contrast, AI data centers demand massive upfront capital per megawatt and carry rapid technology-obsolescence, cooling-design, and leasing risks that infrastructure investors and project lenders are reluctant to underwrite.

Operationally, running high-density AI facilities requires specialized expertise in networking, liquid cooling, strict uptime service-level agreements, and enterprise customer acquisition—capabilities far removed from land siting, permitting, and grid interconnection. Equally important, hyperscalers and dedicated data center operators are power developers' largest, most creditworthy offtake customers; competing with them directly could jeopardize lucrative power supply contracts. For regulated utilities, rate-base and affiliate rules create additional barriers. Instead, power developers capture AI demand more safely by supplying dedicated generation, storage, and grid-ready land through long-term power agreements or joint ventures.

Large power developers usually earn more predictable returns by selling electricity to AI data centers under long-term contracts. Owning the data center would tie up additional capital and expose them to risks they have less experience managing, including construction delays, cooling and network reliability, and whether they can keep the facility leased. Running the AI computing business adds another layer of risk, including rapid chip obsolescence and uncertain demand for computing capacity.

A power developer can still help secure a site, arrange a grid connection, or build generation next to the data center. A hyperscaler or specialist data center operator can then own or operate the facility, while the power developer earns revenue from supplying electricity.
